data.title: Anton Intibus in 1855 on the antiquities around Trnava
data.excerpt: The first Slovak professional archaeologist, Anton Intibus, wrote for the newspaper Slovenské noviny and its supplement Svätozor. Issue 117 of 1855 contains his account of the collection gathered around Trnava by the landowner Ján Hergot – stone mauls, urns, coins and two helmets, one of them with armour and a sword.
data.metaTitle: Anton Intibus (1855) on antiquities near Trnava
data.metaDescription: An account by the first Slovak professional archaeologist Anton Intibus, published in Slovenské noviny in 1855, of the finds made around Trnava.

children.text: The first Slovak professional archaeologist, Anton Intibus, wrote for the newspaper Slovenské noviny and its supplement Svätozor. In issue 117 of 1855 we find the following account, concerning the surroundings of Trnava. The landowner Hergot mentioned in it later donated his collection to Matica slovenská. What became of it afterwards I do not know, but I assume that the objects, if they have survived at all, will be somewhere in Budapest…

blocks.text: On the boundless plains of Trnava there are to be found many antiquities left over from pagan times, and memorials of various kinds from later centuries. That no mention has been made in the public press of these objects, so precious for learning, and that even the inhabitants of the district of Trnava have to this day no knowledge of them, is due partly to the fact that Trnava, like other Hungarian towns, cannot as yet boast of any judicious and impartial topography or chronicle, and partly to the fact that in our homeland very little care has been taken of antiquities and their investigation has been so neglected that many splendid monuments, such as the beautiful Gothic church in Piešťany, have out of sheer ignorance been wiped from the face of the earth; all the more, then, must we admire a man whose station and calling do not indeed permit him to occupy himself more deeply with so exacting a science as the knowledge of antiquities, and who nevertheless does everything in his power to acquire a knowledge of antiquities, and investigates them everywhere in his neighbourhood, collects them and preserves them for the future; this man is Mr Ján Hergot, a landowner formerly resident in Linč and now in Svätý Jur. And since it is well known to me that the said man intends to hand over his whole collection, which he strives to enlarge as abundantly as he can, to some national institution, I shall therefore endeavour first to give an account of it, and then in due time to describe at length the antiquities of the district of Trnava. Now as to Mr Hergot’s collection, it falls into two parts, namely antiquities left over from pagan times, and then memorials deriving from later times. The first consists of stone mauls of various sizes and shapes and of pieces of enormous urns, found on the waste land of Starý Linč, as also of one silver coin, on one side of which there is to be seen, I believe, a winged horse at the gallop. This coin was ploughed up opposite the village of Nová Ves, on the boundary of the Hrnčiarovce–Linč cadastral areas, out of a hill thirty feet high, artificially raised and quite resembling a burial mound. Richer still, however, is Mr Hergot’s collection in objects from Christian times. Of such artificial mounds more rise up about the plains of Trnava; the more considerable of them are: the hill called Rib in the cadastral area of Linč opposite Voderady, then the hill between Rozšindol, Hrnčiarovce and Cifer … left over from the times. He has indeed endeavoured to gather a considerable number of Hungarian, Bohemian and Polish coins found in the district of Trnava, not only of copper and silver but also of gold, such as a ducat of Ladislaus the Posthumous; and not long ago he even purchased for this collection some twenty pieces of ancient Roman coins found at Almáš near Esztergom. The most interesting objects in his collection, however, are two helmets, or helms. One of them, projecting at the top in a semicircle, was found some years ago in the grove of the village of Rozšindol, and it was attached to the steel armour of some man-at-arms in heavy armour, of whose skeleton – and indeed only of the skull – some mouldered remains were still to be found; at his side lay a sword about five feet long but narrow, running out into three edges, as also a ball furnished with seven spikes and a chain; the second of them was dug up in the ramparts at Starý Linč, there where the weirs beyond Trnava once lay; and this one is pointed at the top, resembling the helmets of the Hussites.
